trigger_criteria: Predictable domain outcomes (e.g. invalid credentials, insufficient funds, item out of stock)
decision_rationale: Exceptions destroy performance, break type-level contracts, and force invisible nonlocal control flow jumps.

trigger_criteria: Entities with strict multi-phase transitions where invalid operations must be blocked
decision_rationale: Typestate moves transition validation from runtime exception checks to compile-time compiler guarantees.

trigger_criteria: Multiple combinable business validation rules that evolve independently
decision_rationale: Specification pattern allows unit testing each rule in isolation and combining via .and() / .or().

trigger_criteria: Constructing complex structs, clients, or service objects with >3 optional parameters
decision_rationale: Functional options maintain backward compatibility without breaking existing call sites when new options are added.

trigger_criteria: Multiple interchangeable calculation, sorting, or formatting algorithms
decision_rationale: Closures and typed protocols avoid brittle deep inheritance hierarchies and decouple callers from subclass trees.

trigger_criteria: Raw strings or numbers carrying domain validation invariants (Email, Money, TenantId)
decision_rationale: Value objects and branded types prevent passing an AccountId where a UserId is expected and ensure invariants upon creation.

trigger_criteria: Protecting in-memory shared counters, maps, or caches across concurrent threads
decision_rationale: Mutexes and atomics are significantly faster and simpler for state protection; reserve channels for signaling and streaming.

trigger_criteria: Injecting dependencies into application services and domain handlers
decision_rationale: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, statically verifiable, and effortlessly mockable in unit tests.

trigger_criteria: Processing one of N mutually exclusive message types, domain events, or AST nodes
decision_rationale: Discriminated unions enable compiler exhaustiveness checking, ensuring no unhandled variant escapes to production.

trigger_criteria: Coordinating concurrent access or atomic updates to local files, CLI state, index, cache, or config across processes
decision_rationale: Git lockfile (O_CREAT|O_EXCL + temp write + atomic rename + signal cleanup) eliminates race conditions and partial writes without external infrastructure.

trigger_criteria: Rust application needs generated CRUD and relationship queries from domain models on a verified supported backend
alternate_pattern: SQLx for handwritten SQL; Diesel for a typed query DSL
decision_rationale: Choose for model-first ORM ergonomics rather than a universal quality ranking. Verify required query shapes and relationships plus transaction and migration support on the actual backend; capabilities are not uniform. Native Turso driver uses turso rather than libsql. Model-diff-generated SQL migrations require project-integrated tooling and SQL review; push_schema() is not a production schema-evolution substitute. Sources: https://github.com/tokio-rs/toasty ; https://tokio-rs.github.io/toasty/0.11.0/guide/schema-management.html

trigger_criteria: Rust application needs handwritten SQL or complex database-specific queries with direct SQL control on a supported backend
alternate_pattern: Toasty for model-first ORM; Diesel for a typed query DSL
decision_rationale: SQLx is an async SQL toolkit rather than an ORM. Verify the driver and query-macro schema setup; optional checked macros provide compile-time SQL checks while ordinary runtime queries do not. Verify SQL migrations against the actual engine and deployment. SQLite support alone does not establish native Turso or libSQL integration; do not change engines solely to use SQLx. Source: https://github.com/transact-rs/sqlx

problem_type: Rust typed query DSL and ORM
trigger_criteria: Rust application benefits from composable strongly typed query expressions and an established ORM workflow on a supported backend
alternate_pattern: SQLx for SQL-first control; Toasty for generated model-first queries
decision_rationale: Valid for new projects as well as existing repositories when the typed query DSL fits. Core Diesel is synchronous; diesel-async provides native async PostgreSQL and MySQL connections with SQLite via a sync wrapper. Verify backend features and migration workflow. SQLite support alone does not establish native Turso or libSQL integration. Sources: https://diesel.rs/ ; https://docs.rs/diesel-async/latest/diesel_async/

trigger_criteria: Rust application interfaces directly with SQLite database files without a requirement for an ORM
alternate_pattern: Native turso crate for a Turso engine; an ORM only with verified compatible integration
decision_rationale: Default to libSQL bindings rather than stock SQLite bindings for SQLite-file access. Select local/file mode explicitly; opening a file does not require a cloud account. Verify required extensions and transactions plus any migration workflow. libSQL is a SQLite fork distinct from the native Turso rewrite; file compatibility does not prove driver or ORM interchangeability. Sources: https://docs.turso.tech/libsql ; https://docs.turso.tech/sdk

trigger_criteria: New Rust embedded or local-first relational application fits Turso and does not yet need a larger PostgreSQL ecosystem
alternate_pattern: Toasty when a model-first ORM fits; libsql for direct SQLite-file access; PostgreSQL for concrete ecosystem requirements
decision_rationale: Treat native Turso as the first candidate rather than a measured performance winner. Select the driver for the actual local or sync or remote mode under the SDK matrix. Toasty's native Turso ORM driver is built on turso rather than libsql; verify its required queries and migrations. Do not infer PostgreSQL feature parity or replace an existing compatible engine without authorization. Sources: https://docs.turso.tech/local-development#local-turso-database ; https://docs.turso.tech/sdk
